body_text:
For a predicate $P(x)$ on a domain $D$, the universal statement
$\forall x\in D\,P(x)$ (read *for all $x$ in $D$, $P(x)$*) is
true exactly when $P(a)$ is true for every single element
$a\in D$.

To prove a universal assertion, one must consider an
*arbitrary* element $x \in D$ and prove that $P(x)$ holds using
only the defining properties of $D$, without assuming any
special traits of the chosen element. Conversely, to refute a
universal assertion, one need only exhibit a single
*counterexample*—an element $c \in D$ for which $P(c)$ fails.
